subject: calculus
subtopics: Rolle's theorem: its three hypotheses, its conclusion, and the geometric picture of the horizontal tangent
Lagrange's mean value theorem: its two hypotheses and the tangent parallel to the chord
the equality f(b) - f(a) = f'(c)(b - a) read as an inequality: bounds on a function value from a bound on its derivative
the hypotheses as a test: corners, vertical tangents and discontinuities, and the counterexamples that show the theorem fails without them
finding the point c: the midpoint rule for quadratics, solving f'(c) = average slope, and discarding roots outside the interval
existence against uniqueness: the theorem promises at least one point and says nothing about how many
the three corollaries: zero derivative forces a constant, equal derivatives force a constant difference, and the sign of f' decides monotonicity
root counting: Rolle between two roots of f, and the exactly-one-real-root argument with the intermediate value theorem
Cauchy's extended mean value theorem for two functions, and its relation to L'Hopital's rule
the auxiliary-function construction: building the function that Rolle is applied to
inequalities proved by bounding the derivative between two points
reading a derivative that is zero at one point against a derivative that is zero everywhere

chosen.title: Calculus Volume 1, section 4.4: The Mean Value Theorem
chosen.note: read from the section opening through the proof of the mean value theorem: Rolle's statement and its three-case proof from the extreme value theorem and Fermat's theorem, the explicit warning that differentiability at a single point is critical, the |x| - 1 counterexample, the two worked Rolle examples (x^2 + 2x on [-2, 0] giving c = -1, x^3 - 4x on [-2, 2] giving both plus and minus 2/sqrt(3)), the mean value theorem statement, and its proof by the auxiliary function g(x) = f(x) minus the chord. The corollary subsection further down was beyond the returned extract and nothing is attributed to it
covers: Rolle's theorem: statement, three-case proof, and why each hypothesis is used
the |x| - 1 counterexample that shows the conclusion fails without differentiability
two worked Rolle examples, including one with two interior points
the mean value theorem as the slanted Rolle theorem, with the secant-parallel-to-tangent reading
the proof by the chord-subtraction auxiliary function, which is the construction card 10 teaches
chosen.why: The most complete readable English treatment found this run: it states every hypothesis, proves both theorems, and supplies the counterexample and the worked points the cards need. Chosen over the other textbook pages because its proof of the mean value theorem is the auxiliary-function construction itself, which is a subtopic of this topic and is usually skipped.

chosen.title: Calculus I, section 4.7: The Mean Value Theorem
chosen.channel: Paul's Online Math Notes, Lamar University
chosen.note: read from the opening through the geometric interpretation: Rolle's three hypotheses, the exactly-one-real-root example 4x^5 + x^3 + 7x - 2 (f(0) = -2, f(1) = 10, f'(x) >= 7), the mean value theorem statement in both forms, the explicit note that the theorem does not tell us what c is, and the secant-and-tangent picture. The corollary list further down the page was beyond the returned extract
covers: Rolle's theorem used backwards, by contradiction, to bound the number of real roots
the 4x^5 + x^3 + 7x - 2 example, worked end to end
the statement that the theorem asserts existence and never identifies c
chosen.why: The only readable source that treats root counting through Rolle - the subtopic that the 2014-adjacent GATE statement questions reward and that the OpenStax section does not touch. Its 4x^5 + x^3 + 7x - 2 example is reproduced as card 8's worked example because the numbers are small enough to verify by hand.

chosen.title: 13 Oct - EM - Calculus Part 3, the Rolle's theorem and mean value theorem segment
chosen.note: Hindi-medium live class; the platform's published English AI chapter summary with timestamps was read in full, the lecture itself was not. Chapters used: 10:00-15:00 Rolle's theorem with its conditions and the horizontal-tangent reading; 15:00-20:00 the GATE CS 2014 determinant question solved by Rolle; 20:00-25:00 Lagrange's mean value theorem with the secant picture; 25:00-30:00 Cauchy's extended mean value theorem
covers: Rolle's theorem as GATE states it, with the three conditions and the tangent-parallel-to-the-x-axis reading (10:00-15:00)
the GATE CS 2014 Set 1 Q.6 determinant question solved by Rolle (15:00-20:00)
Lagrange's mean value theorem and the secant-parallel-to-tangent picture (20:00-25:00)
Cauchy's extended mean value theorem in the product form (f(b)-f(a))g'(c) = (g(b)-g(a))f'(c) (25:00-30:00)
chosen.why: The only GATE-oriented teaching of this topic that could be read this run, and the only source that solves a CSE PYQ of the topic. It is Hindi-medium and what was readable is the platform's published English AI chapter summary with timestamps, so the cards take its structure, its order and its worked PYQ, and quote no sentence of the lecturer. It is also the only source for Cauchy's form.

standard_refs: James Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, sections 4.2 and 4.3 (Rolle's theorem and the mean value theorem)
George B. Thomas, Maurice D. Weir and Joel Hass, Thomas' Calculus, chapter 4 (applications of derivatives)
NCERT Mathematics, Class 12, chapter 5 (continuity and differentiability), which contains Rolle's and Lagrange's theorems as the version most Indian candidates meet first
Gilbert Strang et al., OpenStax Calculus Volume 1, section 4.4
GATE 2027 CS syllabus, Engineering Mathematics line 'Limits, continuity and differentiability. Maxima and minima. Mean value theorem. Integration.'
notes: The syllabus names the topic in three words, so the twelve subtopics above are this run's enumeration from the standard treatment (Stewart 4.2-4.3, NCERT chapter 5, OpenStax 4.4) and from the three verified CSE questions, not a quotation from the syllabus.

Only two GATE CSE questions in the whole calculus line turn on a mean value theorem - 2014 Set 1 Q.6 (Rolle) and 2021 Set 2 Q.25 (a bound from Lagrange's form). A third CSE question, 2020 Q.1, is included because the monotonicity corollary is the mean value theorem in use. No CSE question on Cauchy's form or on an MVT inequality was found, so those two cards are P2 and P3 and rest on the standard references.

YouTube served no caption track on any watch page tried this run, so no YouTube lecture is quoted. The GATE-oriented lecture used is recorded from the platform's published English AI chapter summary of a Hindi-medium class and is marked translated.

The non-English material is Hindi-medium (one Knowledge Gate live class) and reaches the cards only through its English AI summary, so the translation sits two layers from the lecture; no card quotes a Hindi sentence.

Both textbook sources were read in part: the extraction service returned the opening through the proof of the mean value theorem, and the corollary subsections beyond that are not quoted. The cards that depend on the corollaries (cards 7, 8 and 12) derive them from the theorem itself, and every number they use is recomputed in scripts/validate.py.

GATE EE 1995's mean-value-theorem bounds question and GATE CSE 2014 Set 2 Q.5 are both genuine previous-year questions of the right shape and both are excluded, with reasons recorded above rather than hidden.
